title: Saint Patrick (17 March)
hookLine: the breastplate prayer: Christ before me, Christ behind me

cards: Green rivers, green beer, plastic hats, a parade down Fifth Avenue. On March 17, people who have never been near Dublin wear green.
Ask someone at the parade who Saint Patrick was and you may hear: he drove the snakes out of Ireland and explained the Trinity with a shamrock. Both stories are later legends.
In his own writing, Patrick never mentions a snake or a shamrock. He left us something better: his own words, and a prayer that carries his name.

teach.b: Patrick wasn't Irish. He was born in Britain, tradition says in the fifth century, the son of a deacon, a boy who by his own account didn't take faith very seriously.
At about sixteen, raiders from Ireland seized him and sold him as a slave.
For six years he herded animals on a cold hillside, and there, alone, he began to pray, he says, a hundred times a day and almost as many at night. Then he escaped, found a ship, and made it home.
And years later, he went back, to the people who had enslaved him, as a bishop, to spend his life among them.
We know because he wrote it down, in a short Latin work called the Confession, which opens with Patrick calling himself a sinner and very unlearned.
Then there's the prayer, called the Breastplate, or the Deer's Cry. Tradition says Patrick sang it while walking past enemies who wanted him dead.
It's written in Old Irish, and scholars who study that language place it after his lifetime; tradition gave it his name. Either way, it's a prayer of armor.
It calls on the Trinity, then the strength of heaven, sun, fire, sea and rock.

teach.h: CHRIST IN EVERY EYE THAT SEES ME.
teach.b: Then the well-known part: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, beneath me, above me.
And it ends looking outward, asking for Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me, and in every eye that sees me.

how: Catholics keep March 17 as the feast of Saint Patrick, a solemnity and holy day in Ireland; some go to Mass before the parades, and the Breastplate prayer is sometimes sung as a hymn.

o: the Irish monk who wrote the Book of Kells

an Irish king who brought the faith home

p: Christ before me, Christ behind me

a later legend. his own writing never mentions snakes.

the Confession, a short account in Latin.

games.q: you're Patrick. you escaped slavery in Ireland and made it home to your family. years later, you dream of the Irish calling you back. what do you do?
o: go back to the land that enslaved you, as a bishop.
games.why: he went back and spent his life among them. his Confession tells of a dream in which the Irish begged him to come and walk among them.

practice: With each slow breath, notice one direction: in front of you, behind you, to your right, to your left, below, above.

If you pray, pray those old lines one direction at a time, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me; if not, simply feel the space around you. Then think of the eyes that will see you today, and the eyes you'll see.

wordCard.voice: Saint Patrick. A Briton, once enslaved in Ireland, who returned as its bishop; patron of Ireland, kept on March 17. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a breastplate; the name for prayers of protection like Saint Patrick's.
